summary: For ages 5–7, teach the brain as the body's CONTROL CENTRE through a repeatable SENSE → BRAIN → MUSCLE loop: the senses send information in, the brain decides, and messages travel out through nerves to tell muscles what to do. Anchor it in a vivid everyday action (eyes see a ball → brain decides 'catch!' → nerves tell the hands to move), and let children generate and act out their own examples so they recognise the same loop in their own catching, turning, and answering. Keep it to the loop and the control-centre idea — no neurons, lobes, or chemistry. Confront the common ideas that the brain is only for thinking, that the heart does the deciding, and that muscles move by themselves.
misconceptions: 'The brain is only for thinking/schoolwork' — missing that it also controls movement and receives all the senses.
'The heart controls the body / feelings come from the heart' — a common young-child idea; the brain is the control centre.
'Muscles move by themselves' — missing that the brain sends the command through nerves.
'The senses work on their own' — not connecting that senses report TO the brain, which then decides.
'The brain and body are separate' — not seeing the constant two-way messaging between them.
'You have to think about everything you do' — (gently) some responses are very fast/automatic, previewing reflexes later.

activities.title: Trigger the loop: sense in, brain decides, muscle out
steps: Choose a situation: a ball flying at you, someone tapping your shoulder, or a friend calling your name.
Start the scene and watch a message light up FROM the sense (eyes, skin, or ears) and race up to the brain.

Watch the brain show a quick 'decide' beat (a little thought bubble), then fire a command DOWN to the right muscles so the character acts — catches the ball, turns to see who tapped, or turns round to answer.
Run a slow-motion replay and narrate each step out loud: 'my eyes told my brain, my brain decided, my brain told my hands.'
Try all three scenarios and notice what stays the same and what changes.
activities.insight: The SAME three-step loop — sense in, brain decides, muscle out — runs every time, just through different senses and body parts, so the brain is the control centre that wires the whole body together.

activities.title: Act out your own loop
steps: Think of something YOU do: catching a ball, scratching when you feel an itch, turning when someone calls your name, or answering a question.
Act it out with your body.
Trace it aloud: 'What did my senses tell my brain? What did my brain decide? What did my brain tell my muscles?'
Do a second example that starts with a different sense (hearing, touch, sight).
activities.insight: The loop isn't just in a model — it runs in the child's own deliberate actions, through whichever sense started it.

activities.title: Feel the helmet: where the brain sits
steps: Feel the hard bone of your skull with your hands.
Talk about why the brain — the body's control centre — is kept inside something hard and strong.
Name one job the brain is doing right now that isn't 'thinking hard', such as keeping you sitting upright.
activities.insight: The brain sits protected inside the skull, which keeps this control centre safe — a simple link between structure and function — and it is busy controlling the body even when you aren't thinking hard.

activities.title: Name the parts of the loop (labelling companion)
steps: On a labelled body, tap the eyes, the brain, the nerves, and a hand muscle to reveal each one's role.
Lift a flap at each step to see 'what message is being sent?'
Put the three steps in order: sense → brain → muscle.
Match a scenario (ball, tap on the shoulder, name called) to the sense that starts it.
activities.insight: Each part of the loop has a role — the sense reports in, the nerves carry the messages, the brain decides, the muscle acts — and the steps happen in a fixed order.

checkQuestion: When you catch a ball someone throws to you, your eyes, your brain, and your hands are all involved. What is your brain's job in catching it, and how does it know to tell your hands to move? Walk me through what happens.
checkAnswer: The eyes see the ball coming and send that information to the brain; the brain — the control centre in your skull — works out where the ball is going and decides to catch it, then sends messages through nerves to the hand muscles telling them to move to the right place. So the brain isn't just for thinking about schoolwork — it takes in what the senses report and controls the body's movements too.
